lessons.title: Common Fungal Diseases: Early Blight, Late Blight, and More
lessons.body:
Fungal diseases are the number one killer of tomatoes in Africa. Early blight starts as small brown spots on lower leaves, often with concentric rings like a target. It spreads upward, causing leaves to yellow and drop. In warm, wet conditions, you can lose a whole crop in two weeks. Late blight is worse: greasy grey-green patches on leaves and stems, white fuzzy mold on the underside, and brown rot on fruit. It spreads fast in cool, rainy weather (15-22Â°C). In Kenya's highlands, late blight can destroy a field in 7 days. Other fungal problems include Septoria leaf spot (small grey spots with dark borders), Fusarium wilt (yellowing on one side, wilting), and powdery mildew (white powder on leaves).

To manage fungal diseases, start with prevention. Plant resistant varieties like 'Defiant' or 'Mountain Magic' for late blight. Space plants 60 cm apart to allow airflow. Water at the base, not on leaves, using drip irrigation or a watering can. Mulch with dry grass to stop soil splash. Remove infected leaves immediately and burn themâdo not compost. If you see early blight, spray copper-based fungicide (e.g., copper oxychloride) every 7-10 days. For late blight, use mancozeb or chlorothalonil at first sign. Always follow label rates: usually 2-3 grams per litre of water. Spray in the evening to avoid leaf burn. Rotate crops: don't plant tomatoes where potatoes or tomatoes grew last season. In dry areas, fungal pressure is lower, but still scout weekly. Remember, fungicides work best before the disease takes hold. If you wait until half the plant is dead, you will lose the crop. Keep a calendar: spray preventively every 10-14 days during rainy season. A simple tool like a knapsack sprayer (15L) costs about $30 and pays for itself. Always wear gloves and a mask when spraying.

lessons.title: Bacterial and Viral Diseases: Identification and Control
lessons.body:
Bacterial and viral diseases have no cure once plants are infected. Your only option is prevention and removing sick plants. Bacterial wilt is common in African soils. It causes sudden wilting of the whole plant while leaves stay green. Cut the stem near the base and put it in a glass of water: if milky white threads ooze out, it's bacterial wilt. There is no chemical cure. Pull the plant and burn it. Do not plant tomatoes there for at least 3 years. Bacterial spot and speck cause small dark spots with yellow halos on leaves and fruit. They spread through rain splash and contaminated tools. Use copper-based bactericides (copper hydroxide) every 7 days, but they only slow it down.

Viral diseases are spread by insects, mainly whiteflies and aphids. Tomato yellow leaf curl virus makes leaves small, yellow, and curled upward. Plants become stunted and produce no fruit. Tomato mosaic virus causes mottled light and dark green leaves, sometimes with fern-like distortion. There is no cure. Control the vectors: use yellow sticky traps (10 per 100 square metres) to catch whiteflies. Spray neem oil (5 ml per litre) or imidacloprid every 14 days. Remove and burn any plant showing virus symptoms immediately. Do not touch healthy plants after handling sick ones without washing hands with soap. For bacterial diseases, avoid overhead watering. Disinfect pruning tools with 10% bleach solution between plants. In Africa, many farmers save seed from infected plants, which spreads viruses. Always buy certified seed from reputable suppliers. If you see virus symptoms, report to your extension officer. Some resistant varieties exist for bacterial wilt (e.g., 'Roma VF'), but not for most viruses. The best strategy is clean seed, vector control, and field hygiene.

lessons.title: Sanitation Practices to Prevent Disease Spread
lessons.body:
Sanitation is your cheapest and most effective disease tool. Most pathogens spread through dirty tools, hands, shoes, and plant debris. Start with clean seedbeds. Sterilise soil by pouring boiling water over it and covering with plastic for 2 days before sowing. Or use a mix of 1 part bleach to 9 parts water to wipe down seedling trays. When working in the field, always start with healthy plants and move to sick ones, never the reverse. Wash hands with soap and water between rows. Wear rubber boots that you can rinse in a bleach solution (1 cup bleach per 10 litres water) at the field entrance. This stops soil-borne diseases like bacterial wilt from moving between plots.

Tools are a major culprit. Pruning shears, hoes, and machetes can carry viruses and bacteria. After each plant, dip tools in 10% bleach or 70% alcohol. Let them air dry. For large farms, keep a bucket of disinfectant at the end of each row. Remove all crop debris after harvest. Do not leave old tomato vines in the fieldâthey harbour late blight and viruses. Burn or bury debris at least 30 cm deep. Compost only if you reach 60Â°C for 3 weeks, which kills most pathogens. But for viral diseases, burn instead. Control weeds like black nightshade and jimsonweed, which host viruses. Keep the field edge clear. If you use stakes, disinfect them with bleach before reuse. In Africa, many farmers share tools. If you borrow a hoe, clean it before use. Also, avoid working in wet fieldsâwet leaves tear easily and invite bacteria. Water early in the day so leaves dry by evening. Mulch with clean straw to prevent soil splash. A simple footbath at the gate (a shallow tray with bleach solution) can reduce spread. Remember: one infected plant can doom a whole crop. Act fast.

lessons.title: Resistant Varieties and Crop Rotation
lessons.body:
The smartest way to fight disease is to grow tomatoes that resist it. Many improved varieties are available in Africa. For late blight, look for 'Defiant', 'Mountain Magic', or 'Iron Lady'âthese have strong resistance. For bacterial wilt, 'Roma VF' and 'Heinz 1370' are good choices. For tomato yellow leaf curl virus, 'Tyking' and 'Fiona' show tolerance. Check with your local agrodealer or extension officer for varieties suited to your region. Resistant does not mean immuneâyou still need good practices, but you will lose fewer plants. When buying seed, ask for certified seed from companies like Seed Co, Kenya Seed, or East-West Seed. Avoid saving seed from hybrid tomatoes; they may not carry resistance. If you must save seed, only from open-pollinated resistant types like 'Roma'. 

Crop rotation is the other pillar. Never plant tomatoes after tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, or eggplantsâthey share the same diseases. Instead, rotate with maize, beans, cabbage, or onions. A good 3-year rotation: Year 1: tomatoes; Year 2: maize; Year 3: beans; Year 4: tomatoes again. This starves soil-borne pathogens like Fusarium and bacterial wilt. In small gardens, rotate in beds: move tomatoes to a different bed each season. If you have no space, plant in containers with fresh potting mix each year. Also, plant marigolds around the borderâthey repel nematodes. Intercrop with onions or garlic; their smell confuses whiteflies and aphids. After harvest, plant a cover crop like lablab or cowpea to improve soil and break disease cycles. Remember, rotation works best when combined with clean seed and sanitation. In Africa, many farmers grow tomatoes continuously on the same plot because of land pressure. If you must, solarise soil: cover with clear plastic for 6 weeks during hot season to kill pathogens. But rotation is cheaper and more reliable.

lessons.title: Using Fungicides and Bactericides Responsibly
lessons.body:
Fungicides and bactericides can save your crop, but only if used correctly. First, identify the disease. Fungal diseases respond to fungicides; bacterial diseases need bactericides (mostly copper-based). Viral diseases have no chemical cure. For early blight, use chlorothalonil (e.g., Bravo) or mancozeb (e.g., Dithane M-45). Mix 2.5 grams per litre of water. For late blight, use metalaxyl plus mancozeb (e.g., Ridomil Gold). Apply every 7-10 days during wet weather. For bacterial spot, use copper hydroxide (e.g., Kocide) at 2 grams per litre. Always read the labelârates vary by product. Use a knapsack sprayer with a fine nozzle. Spray in the evening or early morning to avoid sunburn and bee harm. Wear gloves, a mask, and long sleeves. Never spray on windy days.

Responsible use means rotating chemicals to prevent resistance. Do not use the same fungicide every time. Alternate between groups: e.g., mancozeb (group M3) then chlorothalonil (group M5). For late blight, alternate metalaxyl with cymoxanil. Keep a spray calendar. Do not spray more than every 5 days. Stop spraying 7 days before harvest (pre-harvest interval). Wash vegetables before eating. Store chemicals in a locked box away from children and food. Never mix more than you need. Triple-rinse empty containers and puncture them so they cannot be reused. In Africa, fake pesticides are common. Buy only from licensed agrodealers and check the label for registration numbers. If you use organic methods, copper and neem oil are allowed. Neem oil (5 ml/L) works on powdery mildew and some insects. But copper can build up in soilâuse sparingly. Remember, chemicals are a tool, not a solution. Combine with resistant varieties, sanitation, and rotation. Overuse kills beneficial insects and harms your health. Always follow the labelâit is the law and your best guide.

lessons.title: Managing Soil-Borne Diseases
lessons.body:
Soil-borne diseases are the hardest to control because they live in the ground for years. The main ones are Fusarium wilt, Verticillium wilt, bacterial wilt, and root-knot nematodes. Fusarium wilt causes yellowing and wilting on one side of the plant, often starting on lower leaves. The stem may show brown streaks inside. Verticillium causes similar symptoms but more uniform yellowing. Bacterial wilt causes sudden collapse with green leaves. Nematodes cause stunted growth, yellowing, and galls (lumps) on roots. To diagnose, pull a sick plant and examine roots. If you see galls, it's nematodes. If stem oozes white when cut, it's bacterial wilt. 

Management starts with soil health. Add plenty of organic matter: 2-3 wheelbarrows of well-rotted manure per 100 square metres. This boosts beneficial microbes that fight pathogens. Solarise soil in hot season: wet the soil, cover with clear plastic for 6 weeks. The heat (above 50Â°C) kills many pathogens and nematodes. For bacterial wilt, there is no cureâremove infected plants and do not replant tomatoes there for 3-4 years. For Fusarium and Verticillium, use resistant varieties like 'Roma VF' or 'Celebrity'. For nematodes, plant marigolds (Tagetes) as a cover crop before tomatoes. Their roots release a chemical that kills nematodes. You can also apply neem cake (200 grams per square metre) at planting. Chemical nematicides like fenamiphos are dangerous; use only as last resort. 

Raised beds help with drainage; most soil pathogens thrive in waterlogged soil. Keep pH between 6.0 and 6.8âadd lime if acidic. Rotate with cereals like maize or sorghum. Avoid moving soil between beds on tools or boots. If you have a small garden, use containers with fresh potting mix each season. In Africa, many farmers plant tomatoes in the same spot year after year. Break that cycle. Even a 2-year break with maize or beans can reduce soil-borne diseases by half. Finally, keep records: note which beds had disease, so you can rotate properly. Healthy soil grows healthy plants.

quiz.q: What is a key symptom of early blight on tomato leaves?
options: B) Brown spots with concentric rings
quiz.explanation: Early blight produces brown spots with target-like rings on lower leaves.

quiz.q: Which weather condition favours late blight?
quiz.explanation: Late blight thrives in cool, wet conditions (15-22Â°C) with rain.

quiz.q: What is the best way to water tomatoes to reduce fungal diseases?
quiz.explanation: Watering at the base keeps leaves dry, reducing fungal spore germination.

quiz.q: Which fungicide is recommended for early blight?
quiz.explanation: Mancozeb is a common protectant fungicide for early blight.

quiz.q: How often should you spray preventive fungicide during rainy season?
quiz.explanation: Frequent rains wash off fungicides, so reapply every 10-14 days.

quiz.q: What is a sign of bacterial wilt?
options: B) Sudden wilting with green leaves
quiz.explanation: Bacterial wilt causes rapid collapse while leaves remain green.

quiz.q: How can you test for bacterial wilt?
options: B) Cut stem in water and look for milky ooze
quiz.explanation: Bacterial wilt oozes white threads from cut stems placed in water.

quiz.q: Which insect spreads tomato yellow leaf curl virus?
quiz.explanation: Whiteflies are the main vector for yellow leaf curl virus.

quiz.q: What should you do with a plant showing virus symptoms?
quiz.explanation: There is no cure for viruses, so remove and burn infected plants.

quiz.q: Which tool disinfectant is effective against bacteria and viruses?
quiz.explanation: A 10% bleach solution kills most pathogens on tools.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid working in wet tomato fields?
options: B) Wet leaves tear and invite bacteria
quiz.explanation: Wet leaves are more prone to tearing, which allows bacteria to enter.

quiz.q: What is a good sanitation practice after harvest?
options: B) Burn or bury crop debris
quiz.explanation: Burning or deep burying destroys pathogens that survive in debris.

quiz.q: Which crop should NOT be planted after tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Potatoes share diseases like late blight with tomatoes.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of crop rotation?
quiz.explanation: Rotating with non-host crops reduces pathogen populations in soil.

quiz.q: Which variety is resistant to bacterial wilt?
quiz.explanation: Roma VF has resistance to bacterial wilt (Verticillium and Fusarium).

quiz.q: How long should you wait before planting tomatoes again in soil with bacterial wilt?
quiz.explanation: Bacterial wilt can survive in soil for several years, so a 3-4 year break is needed.

quiz.q: What is the correct rate for mixing copper hydroxide bactericide?
quiz.explanation: Copper hydroxide is typically mixed at 2 g/L for bacterial diseases.

quiz.q: Why should you rotate fungicides?
quiz.explanation: Pathogens can develop resistance if the same chemical is used repeatedly.

quiz.q: What is the pre-harvest interval for most fungicides?
quiz.explanation: Most labels require a 7-day wait before harvest to ensure safe residue levels.

quiz.q: Which of these is a soil-borne disease?
quiz.explanation: Fusarium wilt survives in soil and infects roots.

quiz.q: What does solarisation do to soil?
quiz.explanation: Solarisation heats soil above 50Â°C, killing many pathogens and nematodes.

quiz.q: Which plant can help control nematodes when grown before tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Marigold roots release a substance that repels or kills nematodes.

quiz.q: What is a symptom of root-knot nematode damage?
quiz.explanation: Nematodes cause lumps or galls on tomato roots.

quiz.q: How much well-rotted manure should you add per 100 square metres?
quiz.explanation: Adding 2-3 wheelbarrows of manure improves soil health and suppresses pathogens.

quiz.q: Which pH range is best for tomato growth?
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes grow best in slightly acidic to neutral soil (pH 6.0-6.8).

quiz.q: What should you do if you see whiteflies in your tomato field?
quiz.explanation: Neem oil helps control whiteflies, which spread viruses.

quiz.q: Which of these is a viral disease of tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Tomato mosaic virus is a viral disease with no chemical cure.

quiz.q: Why is it important to buy certified seed?
options: B) It is free of seed-borne viruses
quiz.explanation: Certified seed is tested and free from many seed-borne pathogens.

quiz.q: What is a footbath used for in tomato farming?
options: A) Cleaning shoes to prevent disease spread
quiz.explanation: A bleach footbath disinfects boots and reduces soil-borne disease spread.

quiz.q: Which fungicide group is mancozeb?
quiz.explanation: Mancozeb belongs to FRAC group M3 (multi-site contact fungicide).
